next_text: “A most horrid malicious bloody flame,” he writes, “not like the fine flame of an ordinary fire.” This is the City of London, seen from Bankside, across the Thames. Among the towers stands one dome — and much of this skyline is shaped to keep it in view. We are standing near where Samuel Pepys stood on the second night of the Great Fire. London has burned to the ground twice. Twice, it got the chance to start over. And twice, it rebuilt itself on its old, crooked streets. previous_text: and the people who have lost their homes cannot afford to wait years for it all to be redrawn. So Parliament moves faster. From late February sixteen sixty-seven, a special Fire Court sits at Clifford's Inn, settling disputes between landlords and tenants. In its first year, it decides three hundred and seventy-four cases. A Rebuilding Act sets the rules: outside walls of brick or stone, not timber. And a new duty on coal pays for the City's public buildings. The old street plan stays. Two new streets — King Street and Queen Street — are cut down from the Guildhall toward the river. Rebuilding gets going in sixteen sixty-eight. By the end of sixteen seventy, about six thousand new houses are up — on the same lanes, in brick. Near the bakery, Wren and Hooke raise a column: the Monument. Two hundred and two feet high — exactly the distance to the spot in Pudding Lane where the fire began.
next_text: Fire insurance begins here too. In sixteen eighty, Nicholas Barbon opens the Fire Office. Wren's office rebuilds fifty-one of the City's churches. And on Ludgate Hill, where Old St Paul's stood, work starts in sixteen seventy-five on a new cathedral. The last stone of the lantern is set in seventeen oh-eight — by Wren's son, Christopher. In seventeen eleven, Parliament declares St Paul's complete — three hundred and sixty-five feet, to the top of the cross.

previous_text: For more than two and a half centuries, nothing in London stands taller than the dome.
next_text: By eighteen thirty-one, a new bridge has replaced the medieval one. Wren's steeples ring the dome. Even the river moves. Between eighteen sixty-four and eighteen seventy, Joseph Bazalgette's Victoria Embankment pushes the north bank out into the Thames. In the nineteen thirties, taller office blocks begin to rise near the cathedral, blocking some of its best-known views. But the lanes underneath hardly shift. In nineteen thirty-seven, the cathedral's surveyor, Godfrey Allen, proposes a rule: new buildings must stay low enough to keep the dome in sight from the Thames bridges and the south bank. From nineteen thirty-eight, the City applies it. It is called the St Paul's Heights.
